title: Women’s economic opportunity is constrained less by laws alone than by the weak institutions, policies and enforcement that make formal rights usable
source_unit: World Bank, Women, Business and the Law 2026: Benchmarking Laws for Jobs and Inclusive Growth
geography: 190 economies, assessed across legal frameworks, supportive frameworks and enforcement perceptions

observations.period: 2026 report; global legal and institutional framework for women’s economic opportunity

denominator.unit: economies assessed across 10 topics shaping women's access to jobs and entrepreneurship

legal_framework_score.unit: global average score out of 100 for legal rights supporting women's economic equality

supportive_framework_score.unit: global average score out of 100 for policies and institutions needed to make rights effective

enforcement_perception_score.unit: global average score out of 100 based on legal experts' perceptions of enforcement

full_equality.unit: economies granting women the full set of measured legal economic rights

observations.method: World Bank Women, Business and the Law 2026 index using three pillars—legal frameworks, supportive frameworks and enforcement perceptions—across 10 topics.
observations.uncertainty: Index scores summarize coded legal and institutional indicators and expert perceptions; they do not directly measure individual experience, compliance, labor-market outcomes or causal effects of reform.
observations.subgroup: Women seeking paid work, entrepreneurship, assets, childcare, safety, retirement security and equal treatment across 190 economies.
observations.counterinterpretation: Formal legal change can still matter by establishing claims, standards and institutional direction even when implementation is incomplete.

observations.period: 2026 report; distribution of legal equality and economic opportunity

denominator.unit: economies assessed in Women, Business and the Law 2026

women_near_full_equality.unit: percent of women living in economies close to full legal equality

rights_gap.value: women globally enjoy about two-thirds of the legal rights of men

economic_potential.unit: percent potential increase in global GDP from closing the gender gap in employment and entrepreneurship

observations.method: World Bank global comparison of legal equality and modeled economic implications of closing gender gaps in employment and entrepreneurship.
observations.uncertainty: The GDP estimate is a modeled potential, not a forecast or guaranteed return; cross-economy legal scores do not capture within-country differences, informal institutions or household constraints.
observations.subgroup: Women and men participating in labor markets, firms, entrepreneurs, households and policymakers assessing inclusive growth.
observations.counterinterpretation: Removing legal barriers is necessary but not sufficient; care burdens, norms, capital access, safety, discrimination and labor demand can still constrain participation.

denominator.unit: economies monitored for legal reforms strengthening women's economic opportunities

reforming_economies.unit: economies enacting reforms strengthening women's economic opportunities between 2023 and 2025

legal_reforms.unit: legal reforms enacted across the 68 economies between 2023 and 2025

implementation_gap.value: legal reform is not equivalent to supportive institutions or effective enforcement

observations.method: World Bank tracking of reforms and comparison across legal, supportive and enforcement-perception pillars.
observations.uncertainty: Reform counts do not measure the substantive effect, implementation quality, enforcement consistency, public awareness or women's actual economic outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Women in reforming and non-reforming economies, public authorities, courts, regulators, employers and civil-society organizations.
observations.counterinterpretation: Incremental reform can create institutional learning and improve opportunity over time even when aggregate scores remain low.

observations.period: 2026 report; safety, care and enterprise as economic infrastructure

denominator.unit: economies assessed across the working-life topics in Women, Business and the Law 2026

weakest_topics.value: safety, entrepreneurship and childcare are among the weakest areas of measured support for women's economic participation

life_cycle_scope.value: safety, mobility, work, pay, marriage, parenthood, childcare, entrepreneurship, assets and pension

economic_infrastructure.value: legal rights require courts, regulatory bodies, administrative systems, childcare and other supportive institutions to become usable opportunities

observations.method: World Bank topic-level analysis and expanded WBL 2.0 framework combining formal rights with supportive systems and enforcement perceptions.
observations.uncertainty: Topic-level scores are comparative diagnostics and do not reveal the full causal chain from law to safety, care access, entrepreneurship, employment or income.
observations.subgroup: Women balancing paid work, care, mobility, safety, entrepreneurship, asset ownership and retirement security.
observations.counterinterpretation: Supportive systems may expand opportunity, but their effects depend on financing, social norms, employer practice, labor demand and access for informal or marginalized workers.

related_sources.claim: World Bank WBL 2026 datasets and reproducibility packages.
World Bank document metadata and official report record.

boundary: This record adds a law-to-capability and gendered economic-opportunity route. It is a global legal and institutional benchmark, not respondent-level data, a measure of lived discrimination, a causal evaluation of reforms, or proof that legal equality automatically produces equal employment, income or entrepreneurial outcomes.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official World Bank WBL 2026 report page, flagship report page, data page, reproducibility package and full report PDF were reviewed for the three-pillar framework, global scores, reform counts, topic gaps and modeled economic potential; the full report PDF was hashed.
